chicken-fillet-sandwich-fried-on-white-b.title: Chicken Fillet Sandwich, Fried, on White Bun with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The sandwich consists of a fried chicken fillet, melted cheese, fresh vegetables and sauce, placed between a split white bun. It is a popular fast‑food item served in cafés and quick‑service restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The chicken fillet is usually grilled or deep‑fried, giving it a golden crust.
White buns often contain a small amount of sugar and dairy, making them soft and slightly sweet.
Melted cheese is commonly used because it spreads quickly and binds the ingredients.
Chicken sandwiches gained popularity in the United States in the 1970s as a lighter alternative to beef burgers.
Some versions add lettuce, tomato, and pickles for extra freshness and crunch.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, chicken fillet has less saturated fat.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sandwich provides a quick source of calories, convenient for active lifestyles.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salt used in the bun and sauce may be a concern for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Trans fats in fried fillet
items.content: If the fillet is deep‑fried, trans fats may form, which are undesirable with frequent consumption.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor salmonella; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat with hands, but you can cut it in half and add extra sauce if desired. It is often served with fries or a fresh side salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in plastic to prevent the bun from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Swordfish (Xiphias gladius) is a large oceanic fish with a distinctive long, flat bill that resembles a sword. It inhabits warm waters worldwide and can weigh up to 650 kg. The flesh is firm, white, and mildly flavored, commonly used for steaks, sashimi, and canning.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Swordfish can reach speeds of up to 60 km/h thanks to its powerful tail and streamlined body.
The bill can exceed 1 m in length, though it is usually shorter.
It can dive deeper than 600 m, where water temperature is around 4 °C.
Swordfish is one of the fastest predators in the open ocean.
In many cultures its meat is considered a delicacy, served as grilled, baked, or fried steaks.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Swordfish provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other marine fish, swordfish has a low saturated fat content, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: The flesh contains EPA and DHA omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Swordfish provides selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting antioxidant defenses and bone health.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: As a large predatory fish, swordfish can accumulate mercury; intake should be limited for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to seafood may react to swordfish meat.

items.title: Raw fish
items.content: Raw or undercooked swordfish may harbor parasites; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Swordfish is commonly grilled, baked, or pan‑seared. 2–3 cm thick steaks cook for 4–5 minutes per side. The flesh is also suitable for sashimi when properly treated. Serve with a squeeze of lemon or a drizzle of olive‑oil‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh swordfish in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C, wrapped in plastic, for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator before cooking.

macaroni-or-noodles-with-cheese-made-fro.title: Macaroni or noodles with cheese, reduced fat mix

content.title: About
content.content: The dry packaged mix “Macaroni with cheese” contains pasta or noodles and a reduced‑fat cheese sauce powder. Preparation takes 5‑7 minutes: just add hot water, stir, and let it sit. The product is convenient for quick meals at home, in the office, or on the go.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese sauce is fortified with calcium and vitamin D to offset the lower fat content.
A special dry‑sieving process preserves the cheese flavor without needing butter.
The package has a long shelf life – up to 12 months when stored in a dry, cool place.
Whole‑grain flour is often added, increasing dietary fiber content.
Leading brands use pasta shapes that hold the sauce better.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese sauce provides a substantial portion of the daily calcium requirement, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Compared with traditional mac and cheese, this mix contains roughly half the fat, making it more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta adds fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Quick preparation
items.content: Short cooking time helps retain more nutrients than prolonged boiling.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cheese sauce contains dairy proteins that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Dry sauces often have added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional wheat pasta contains gluten, so the product is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: Although fat is reduced, the mix may contain food additives and flavor enhancers that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour hot water (about 200 ml) over the packet, stir, cover, and let stand for 5‑7 minutes. For extra flavor you can add fresh vegetables, herbs, or a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened packet in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, seal the bag tightly to prevent moisture ingress.

content.title: About
content.content: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a bright green, leafy herb native to the Mediterranean region, with a fresh, slightly peppery flavor. The two main types are curly parsley and flat-leaf (Italian) parsley. Parsley is used as a garnish and as a flavoring in salads, sauces, soups, marinades, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parsley belongs to the same plant family as carrots, celery, dill, and cilantro.
Flat-leaf parsley has a stronger flavor than curly parsley and is preferred for cooking.
Parsley root, a relative of the herb, is also eaten as a vegetable.
Parsley is a key ingredient in tabbouleh, chimichurri, and gremolata.
Parsley has been used as a culinary and traditional herb since ancient times.

items.title: Very rich in vitamin K
items.content: Parsley is an excellent source of vitamin K, which supports normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and vitamin A
items.content: Parsley contains vitamin C and carotenoids that support the immune system and vision.

items.title: Provides folate and iron
items.content: These nutrients support cell function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains plant compounds
items.content: Parsley contains flavonoids such as apigenin and luteolin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Adds flavor with few calories
items.content: Parsley brightens dishes without adding many calories.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Parsley contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Pregnancy and concentrated products
items.content: Parsley in normal food amounts is generally fine, but large medicinal amounts, concentrated oil, or supplements should be avoided during pregnancy unless advised by a healthcare professional.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Parsley contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Allergic reactions and skin sensitivity
items.content: Parsley belongs to the same family as celery and carrots, so cross-reactions are possible, and handling large amounts in sunlight may cause skin irritation in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh parsley can be chopped into salads, soups, sauces, marinades, eggs, and grains, or blended into pesto, chimichurri, and green juices. Add it at the end of cooking to keep its flavor and color. The stems also have flavor and can be used in stocks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh parsley in the refrigerator, with the stems in a glass of water loosely covered or wrapped in a damp paper towel in a bag, where it keeps for about a week. Chopped parsley can be frozen. Store dried parsley in an airtight container in a cool, dark place.

soup-sopa-or-caldo-de-pollo.title: Soup, sopa or caldo de pollo

content.title: About
content.content: Soup is a liquid dish made from broth, water or milk with added meat, fish, vegetables, grains and spices. The "caldo de pollo" version is a traditional chicken broth popular in Latin American cuisine, often served with noodles, rice or potatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soup is considered one of the oldest dishes: archaeological evidence shows its existence over 5,000 years ago.
There are hundreds of soup varieties worldwide, from Japanese miso to French onion.
Chicken broth (caldo de pollo) is often used as a home remedy for colds because of its warming and hydrating properties.
Traditional Mexican "sopa de tortilla" is made with fried corn tortillas, tomatoes, chilies and chicken broth.
In some cultures soup is served as a starter, while in others it is a main course.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken broth provides easily digestible protein that supports tissue repair and immune function.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm bowl of soup helps replenish body fluids, especially beneficial during illness.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Soups made with vegetables are high in vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Warm liquid stimulates gastric secretions, making digestion easier.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Most broths are low‑calorie, making them suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Broths can be high in sodium, which may raise blood pressure in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some people may have allergic reactions to chicken meat or the spices used in the soup.

items.title: Contamination
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to bacterial growth, especially in meat‑based broths.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some ready‑made soups contain added MSG, which can cause headaches in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve soup hot in a deep bowl or mug. Garnish with fresh herbs, lemon wedges, croutons, grated cheese or raw vegetables. For a heartier meal add noodles, rice, beans or potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage freeze in portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.

tuna-casserole-with-vegetables-and-mushr.title: Tuna casserole with vegetables and mushroom sauce, no noodles

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna casserole with vegetables and mushroom sauce, no noodles is a hearty dish where tuna fillet is combined with a mix of vegetables (broccoli, carrots, bell pepper) and a creamy mushroom sauce made from cream and mushrooms. Instead of traditional noodles, cauliflower or simply extra vegetables are used, making the meal lighter and low‑carb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart and brain health.
Mushroom sauce is often prepared with cream, broth, and a touch of flour, giving a velvety texture without cheese.
A noodle‑free casserole fits well into keto and low‑carb diets.
Vegetables retain most of their vitamins when lightly sautéed before baking.
In the United States, similar casseroles are traditionally made with pasta, but vegetable replacements have become popular in recent years.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A single serving of tuna delivers about 30 g of complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Skipping noodles and using vegetables keeps the dish suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Broccoli, carrots, and bell pepper add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium, and fiber.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Mushrooms contain beta‑glucans that may enhance the immune response.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to marine fish, including tuna.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; pregnant women and young children should limit intake.

items.title: High sodium in canned tuna
items.content: If using canned tuna, choose low‑sodium varieties.

items.title: Calorie‑dense sauce
items.content: Cream and butter increase calories; lighter alternatives can be used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot, cut into portions. It pairs well with a simple green salad or fresh tomatoes. Garnish with chopped parsley or dill for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave, covering with foil to prevent drying.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable oil NFS is a high‑quality food oil obtained from a blend of rapeseed, sunflower and soybeans. It has a neutral taste and aroma, suitable for frying, baking and salad dressings. The oil features a high smoke point, making it safe for high‑temperature cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS stands for “Neutral Flavor and Stability”.
The blend provides a more balanced fatty‑acid profile than single‑source oils.
Low polyphenol content gives the oil a long shelf life.
In Russia and CIS countries NFS is widely used in catering and food manufacturing.

items.title: Source of polyunsaturated fatty acids
items.content: The oil contains omega‑6 and a modest amount of omega‑3 fatty acids, which are important for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with animal fats, NFS oil has less saturated fat, helping to lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Fats provide a concentrated source of energy needed for active lifestyles.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy proteins may be present and can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Oxidation if stored improperly
items.content: Exposure to heat and light can cause the oil to become rancid, affecting taste and nutritional quality.

items.title: High omega‑6 content
items.content: Excessive omega‑6 intake without adequate omega‑3 may promote inflammatory processes.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: The oil is suitable for frying, baking, making sauces and dressing salads. It can be used in dough, marinades and Asian dishes. For best flavor, store in a dark place and avoid heating above 200 °C.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the oil in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. After opening, use within 6 months. Discard if a rancid odor develops.
